Ten to thirty inches of heavy snow were reported over the higher elevations and at ski resorts. Gusty winds and blowing snow caused additional travel problems on Interstate 80 and Highway 50.
Snow amounts up to 10 inches were reported over the higher elevations of Shasta County.
CHP closed the west bound lane of Highway 70 in the Rich Bar area due to a rock slide resulting from heavy rainfall on a burn area.
The Glenn County Sheriff Office reported nickel-size hail in Fruto.

Hail covered the roads and a grain field was flattened by at least penny-size hail. The hills were whitened by hail. In addition, there were 0.57 inches of rain in Artois in one hour. An NWS employee on a storm survey the next day measured hail to 1.25 inches in diameter, with depths of the hail exceeding 6 inches.
Penny-size hail fell near Artois.

events.cz_name: MOUNTAINS SOUTHWEST SHASTA COUNTY TO NORTHERN LAKE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow fell over the southern Cascade and northern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Snow levels over the area started at 6000 feet then fell to around 2500 feet by Wednesday. Snowfall amounts were up to 12 inches.

Local law enforcement reported one fatality and numerous accidents in the Redding area due to heavy rain and local flooding. Total rainfall amounts up to 4.46 inches were reported by COCORAHS observers. Clogged and overwhelmed storm drains caused numerous road and business closures across the area. A 25 year old man was reported to have drowned after falling into Calaboose Creek. His body was found in the creek near Cypress Ave.
Heavy rain caused road closings due to minor flooding of several county roads.
Minor flooding of rural county roads.
Minor flooding of rural county roads.
Minor flooding of rural county roads.

Heavy snow fell over the northern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Snow levels over the area started at 6500 feet and then fell to around 3000 feet by Wednesday. Some storm total snowfall amounts include 60 inches of snow at Blue Canyon, 53 inches at Sierra at Tahoe, 57 to 64 inches at Boreal, 53 to 64 inches at Kirkwood, and 49 to 68 inches at Sugar Bowl. Blowing snow brought zero visibility to Interstate 80 on the 3rd, and the CHP closed a 60 mile stretch from Applegate to the Nevada-California border. There were 10 tractor trailers reported jacknifed along I-80. Other area mountain roads such as Highway 50 required snow chains.
Hail fell up to 3 inches deep, with some stones measuring up to penny-size.
CHP reported up to 2 inches of hail covering Interstate 5.
Lighting struck a dentist office, damaging a swamp cooler on the roof, the office computer, and the phone system.

Hail blanketed the ground to 2 inches deep on Bowman Rd. near Interstate 5.  Most of the hail was pea size. There were 3 car accidents reported in the area on Interstate 5 during the hail event, with two ambulances dispatched.

Heavy snow fell over the southern Cascade and northern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Snow levels over the area started at 6000 feet then fell to around 2500 feet by Wednesday. Snowfall amounts were up to 12 inches.

Heavy snow fell over the southern Cascades and northern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Snow levels over the area started at 6000 feet and then fell to around 2500 feet by Wednesday. Snowfall amounts 6 to 12 inches.

Heavy snow fell over the southern Cascades and northern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Snow levels over the area started at 6000 feet and then fell to around 2500 feet by Wednesday. Snowfall amounts up to 10 inches.

A gustnado developed ahead of a line of showers moving through the city of Woodland. The discontinuous damage path was about 1700 feet long and 20 feet across. A tree two feet in diameter was uprooted, a section of metal bleachers were moved, and several tents were damaged. There was minor damage to three mobile homes in a nearby mobile home park, with porches pulled off and large flower pots knocked over.
Snow amounts up to a foot fell over the higher mountains. Gusty winds were reported lowering visibilities on mountain passes.
Snow amounts up to a foot fell over the higher mountains. Gusty winds were reported lowering visibilities on mountain passes.
Snow amounts up to 7 inches fell over the higher mountains. Gusty winds were reported lowering visibilities on mountain passes.
Snow amounts up to a foot fell over the higher mountains. Gusty winds were reported lowering visibilities on mountain passes.
Heavy snow fell in the higher mountains, with around 1 foot recorded at lower Lassen Peak.  Travel on area roads was affected.

Heavy snow fell over the higher mountains with amounts over 2 feet at the ski resorts. Around 12 to 14 inches was recorded Ebbetts Pass and Echo Summit.  Chain controls were in effect for Interstate 80 and Highway 50.
Scattered thunderstorms over the area brought hail to Shasta County. A spotter reported hail 1/4 to 3/4 inch covering the ground in the Shingletown area near Highway 44.
Hail to the size of quarters, strong gusty winds, and heavy rain was reported west of Interstate 5 near Corning.

A wildfire started on July 26th along the Middle Fork of the Stanislaus River, near Mt. Knight, in Stanislaus County.  The fire had burned 2734 acres by the end of July and continued to burn into August.  It brought multiple local road closures and smoke to the nearby area.
Lassen Volcanic National Park rangers reported quarter sized hail.
A Co-operative observer estimated hail from dime to penny sized.
The Elephant Wildfire burned 445 acres of woodland.  Highway 70 travel was limited at one point to one way traffic with a pilot car, causing travel delays.

Thunderstorm lightning strikes starting at least 43 fires in Lassen National Forest on August 1st. The largest of the Hat Creek Complex fires were the Sugarloaf, Brown, and the Butte fires. There were 11,269 acres of forest burned in the Complex.  Other impacts included evacuations of campgrounds in the Hat Creek Recreation area, road closures of portions of State Highway 89 and State Highway 44, and the closure of the Pacific Crest Trail.
There were 6130 acres of forest burned in rugged terrain along the Middle Fork of the American River.  Local forest service roads were closed due to the fire, as were several campgrounds.

Thunderstorm lightning strikes started numerous fires in Shasta County on the evening of August 1st. The SHU Complex consisted of 40 fires, with the largest being the Gomez, Cave, Cassel, the Goose, and the Chalk fires.  Dozens of homes were evacuated and a number of area roads were closed. There were 17,623 acres of forest burned prior to containment on August 17th.  This fire complex included burned acreage in CA-Z013.

Thunderstorm lightning strikes started numerous fires in Shasta County on the evening of August 1st. The Complex consisted of 40 fires, with the largest being the Gomez, Cave, Cassel, the Goose, and the Chalk fires. Dozens of homes were evacuated, and a number of area roads were closed. There were 17,623 acres of forest burned prior to containment on August 17th.  This fire complex included burned acreage in CA-Z014.

A woman was struck by lightning while carrying a large umbrella at a softball game at the San Joaquin Regional Sports Complex in Stockton.  Additional reports suggest the lightning hit about 30 feet away from her.  The woman suffered minor injuries.

Lightning started a number of fires over the northern Sierra Nevada Mountains including the Telegraph Fire near Copperopolis (200 acres) and the San Antonio Fire near Arnold (5 acres), both located in Calaveras County.  The other fires were small and quickly extinguished.

The Silver Fire burned 307 acres of forest in steep terrain in the Plumas National Forest in Plumas County.  The fire burned to about 10 miles west of Quincy and was also near Silver Lake and the community of Meadow Valley.

Downtown Sacramento recorded 3.04 inches of rain on the 13th, which was the second highest 24 hour rain amount to occur in the month of October and the 11th highest of all time.  An additional 0.20 inches fell on the 14th.  Other towns in the vicinity received two to three inches for the storm total.||Numerous storm drains clogged, causing local street flooding.  The most notable was  along the section of Interstate 5 going through downtown Sacramento, which caused travel problems for many hours.  ||Several buildings were damaged from the heavy rain including a Filco store in Citrus Heights that suffered a roof collapse from water buildup. Minor flooding was also reported to have damaged nearby homes.||Peak wind gusts of 48 mph were recorded at Sacramento Executive Airport on the 13th.  Hundreds of trees and large branches fell, damaging numerous cars and causing power outages for approximately 124,000 customers in the Sacramento area.

Stockton Airport recorded 1.46 inches of rain which was the daily record for October 13th.  This broke the previous record of 0.76 inches set in 1962.  The heavy rain caused numerous storm drains to clog and resulted in local street flooding.||Wind gusts up to 49 mph were recorded at Stockton Airport on the 13th.  Numerous trees, large tree branches, and power lines were reported down which resulted in power outages to at least 9,000 customers in San Joaquin County.

Travis Air Force Base recorded 4.75 inches of rain on the 13th. Vacaville recorded 4.23 inches, which was a 24 hour record record for that site.  The heavy rain resulted in numerous storm drains becoming clogged which caused local street flooding. ||Wind gusts up to 48 mph were recorded at Vacaville Airport on the 13th.  Numerous trees, large tree branches, and power lines were reported down which resulted in power outages to at least 14,000 customers in Solano County.

Various locations in Calaveras County reported 4 to 6 inches of rain on the 13th.  This resulted in numerous storm drains becoming clogged which caused local street flooding.||Strong, gusty winds brought down large numbers of trees, large branches, and power lines which resulted in power outages to many customers in Calaveras County.

Stirling City recorded 4.96 inches of rainfall on the 13th and Chico recorded 1.35 inches.  The heavy rain caused numerous storm drains to clog which resulted in local street flooding.||Strong, gusty winds brought down large numbers of trees, large branches, and power lines which resulted in power outages to at least 2,600 customers in Butte County.

Heavy rain fell in Nevada County on the 13th.  This caused numerous storm drains to clog which resulted in some local street flooding.||Strong, gusty winds peaking near 40 mph brought down large numbers of trees, large tree branches, and power lines which resulted in power outages to at least 10,900 customers in Nevada County.

Redding Airport recorded 1.37 inches of rainfall on the 13th.  Clear Lake (3300 feet elevation) recorded 7.52 inches of rain in the 24 hour period ending at 5 pm on the 13th.  Several automated gages and CoCoRaHS observers in the higher elevations of northern Shasta County reported storm total rainfall amounts on the 13th and 14th exceeding 12 inches.||Several storm gutters and drains were clogged in Redding, with some local street flooding occurring.||There were gusty winds up to 51 mph, with large numbers of trees and branches reported down in Shasta County, causing at hundreds of customers to lose power. A number of cars were damaged by falling trees.||Snow caused the closure of Highway 89 in Lassen Volcanic National Park, where there was more than 6 inches of accumulation at 8,500 feet elevation.

Red Bluff Airport recorded 1.95 inches of rainfall on the 13th. ||Strong, gusty winds peaking at 53 mph brought down numerous trees, large branches, and power lines which resulted in power outages in Tehama County.

Modesto Airport recorded 1.57 inches of rainfall on the 13th, which was a record for the date.  This broke the old record of 0.76 inches set in 1962.  The heavy rain caused minor street flooding, primarily as a result of clogged storm drains.||Strong, gusty winds peaking at 47 mph at Modesto Airport brought down hundreds of trees, large tree branches, and power lines resulting in power outages in Stanislaus County.  Falling trees also badly damaged numerous cars and houses.
The Oasis Fire burned 1575 acres in the Cache Creek Wilderness in eastern Lake County.  There were 4 firefighters injured, but no structures damaged or destroyed.

Redding Police reported Boulder Creek running out of its banks, flooding an adjacent RV park and apartment complex.  Evacuations were ordered and minor damage was done to several RVs. Clogged storm drains resulted in the flooding of a nearby intersection to nearly three feet deep, in which several cars stalled.
Eight inches of snow were reported at Harkness Flat and at Lower Lassen Peak, with fifteen inches measured at Meadow Lake. Winds gusted to 38 mph at Manzanita Lake.

More than a foot of snow was reported in the higher elevations of the northern Sierra Nevada Mountains, with up to 15 inches measured near Donner Pass.  Winds gusted to 50 to 60 mph over higher elevations which resulted in poor visibilities. Highway travel on Interstate 80, US 50, and the other trans-Sierra pass roads was impacted.

A gustnado was sighted just southwest of Wheatland ahead of an approaching thunderstorm.  The gustnado was initially reported as a tornado.  No damage was reported nor discovered during a damage survey.
CHP reported a woman injured when lightning struck power lines and went through a video game system she was playing.

Heavy snow fell in the northern Sierra Nevada Mountains, with up to 3 feet of accumulation. Thirty six inches of snow were recorded at Lake Alpine, 35 inches recorded 10 miles west of Soda Springs, and 21 inches at Pacific House.  ||The heavy snow along with gusty winds produced hazardous road conditions over the Sierra Nevada passes.  There were temporary road closures on long stretches of Interstate 80 and Highway 50 due to low snow levels.

Rain turned to snow in the early morning hours in Sacramento and the eastern suburbs, starting around 200 AM and ending by 500 AM.  An inch of snow was measured in Folsom, a half inch in Carmichael and Loomis, and a trace of snow was recorded in Roseville and Granite Bay.  Snow was observed falling in Sacramento but with no accumulation. Area roads were slippery and a number of car accidents occurred.
Thirteen separate collisions caused a 33 vehicle pileup in dense fog on Interstate 5 near Lodi.  There were 16 injuries reported, one of them serious.

A hard freeze caused numerous pipes and sprinkler systems to burst over the northern Sacramento Valley, causing water damage to homes and businesses. At least 50 pipe burst incidents were reported in Red Bluff and twenty one in Corning.||An all time record low temperature of 16 degrees was set on December 9th at Redding Municipal Airport. The previous record was 17 degreees, set on January 13, 1930.

A hard freeze caused pipes and sprinkler systems to burst throughout the central Sacramento Valley, causing water damage to homes and businesses. ||Some crop damage to mandarin oranges, lemons, olives, and avocados was also reported.

A hard freeze caused pipes and sprinkler systems to burst throughout the southern Sacramento Valley, causing water damage to homes and businesses. ||There were nine water main breaks reported in Sacramento, with eighty two  customers reporting problems with leaking pipes. There were five broken pipes reported in Roseville.

A hard freeze caused pipes and sprinkler systems to burst throughout the Motherlode area, causing water damage to homes and businesses. There were 287 residential breaks reported in El Dorado County alone.  In Nevada County, the Rood Government Center had flooding due to a burst sprinkler system, resulting in the evacuation of 400 employees.  In addition, a bank in Nevada City was also evacuated due to damaged ceiling panels caused by a broken sprinkler system pipe.
A hard freeze caused pipes and sprinkler systems to burst throughout the northern San Joaquin Valley area, causing water damage to homes and businesses.
Heavy snow fell above 5000 feet with up to two feet of new accumulation.

Heavy snow fell over the higher mountain passes and peaks.  Snow levels were near 5000 feet with a foot or more of snow measured above 7000 feet.
Snow amounts up to a foot were reported above 5000 feet, with 10 inches of new snow measured at Mineral.  The heavy snow and gusty winds resulted in hazardous travel.

Snow amounts of 1 to 3 feet were reported above 5000 feet at northern Sierra Nevada mountain ski resorts and SNOTEL sites.  Fourteen inches was measured at Blue Canyon and 33 inches was measured at Soda Springs.  A wind gust to 45 mph was reported at Blue Canyon. The heavy snow and gusty wind resulted in hazardous travel over mountain roads and passes.
Penny size hail covered the ground to 2 inches deep near Vacaville, causing numerous car accidents.

Wind gusts to 60 mph were measured at Oroville Airport.
Snow amounts of 7 to 10 inches were reported.  The heavy snow and gusty winds resulted in hazardous travel.

Seven inches of snow fell at Mineral, causing travel difficulties on higher mountain roads.

Seven to twelve inches of snow fell at area ski resorts above 5000 feet, with 17 inches measured above 8000 feet. The snow along with locally gusty winds causing travel difficulties on higher mountain pass roads such as Highway 50 and Interstate 80.
Wind gusts to 57 mph and sustained winds to 44 mph were measured at Stockton Airport.  The wind knocked out power to 14000 customers in the area.
Snow amounts of up to 8 inches fell over the higher mountain ridges.

At approximately 1:17 pm an EF1 tornado developed near the town of Latrobe in El Dorado County, which is about four miles south of El Dorado Hills.  The maximum wind speed of the tornado was estimated at 100 mph with a damage path of two miles.  No injuries or fatalities have been reported.  There was damage to the roof of one commercial building, a single power pole, a water tank, and to numerous trees.||Witness reports were crucial to the conclusion of the damage assessment as there was not a great deal of damage from which to distinguish between tornadic, downburst, or straight line winds.  The conclusion of an EF1 designation was based primarily upon the damage caused to the oak trees in the damage path.

At approximately 3:05 pm  an EF0 tornado touched down in a pasture about 2 miles west of downtown Maxwell.  The pasture is located just north of Maxwell Sites Rd., between McDermott Rd. and Danley Rd.  There was no damage observed, but several witnesses observed a brief touchdown in the grassy field, which is used as pasture for a herd of buffalo.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.

At approximately 3:00 pm an EF0 tornado touched down about a mile WSW of downtown Williams in Colusa County, near the intersection of Hwy 20 and Davis Road.  The maximum wind speed of the tornado was estimated at 80 mph with a damage path of three quarters of a mile.  The damage path was in an east-northeast direction.  No injuries nor fatalities have been reported.  The tornado damaged six homes, an out-building, two vehicles, and a home radio tower.

At approximately 3:52 pm an EF0 tornado touched down less than a mile south of downtown Rockville in Solano County, near Rockville Road and Suisun Valley Road.  The maximum wind speed of the tornado was estimated at 70 mph with a damage path of 200 yards.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.  The tornado caused roof damage to two small businesses and damaged several trees, fences, and signs.

At approximately 3:05 pm an EF0 tornado touched down at the Mather Field Industrial Park, immediately north of Mather Field.  The maximum wind speed of the tornado was estimated at 75 mph with a damage path of one third of a mile.  The damage path was in a northeast direction.  No injuries nor fatalities have been reported.  Damage was to a few trees including a large evergreen tree, broken road signs, and broken windows to multiple cars.

The first and northernmost tornado in the outbreak developed east of the town of Artois in Glenn County at approximately 5:08 pm and moved east-northeast, passing south of the town of Chico in Butte County.  It caused significant damage to an almond grove in Glenn County and less significant damage to farm implements, roofing materials, and another almond grove across its path.  The rating of an EF1 was based upon the uprooting of hundreds of almond trees with a few instances of broken large branches and trunks.  The estimated highest wind speed (3 second gust) based upon damage with this tornado is 95 mph.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.

The second tornado of the outbreak developed northeast of downtown Willows in Glenn County at approximately 5:12 pm.  It moved east-northeast and passed just south of the town of Durham in Butte County.  It caused significant damage to almond groves in Butte County, as well as destroyed one out building, damaged an open barn, and caused roofing damage to two other structures.  The rating of an EF1 was based upon the uprooting of thousands of almond trees with many instances of broken large branches and trunks and the physical lifting and carrying of several large trees by five to ten feet.  The estimated highest wind speed (3 second gust) based upon damage with this tornado is 105 mph.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.

The third tornado in the outbreak developed approximately northwest of Oroville in Butte County at approximately 645 pm and moved northeast.  It caused significant damage to a ranch property near the intersection of Table Mountain Road and Hwy 70 including the destruction of a large, well built garage and significant damage to an open barn.  The rating of an EF2 was based upon the destruction of the garage, though evidence was found of the footing boards being bolted to the slab in the front portion of the structure.  The estimated highest wind speed (3 second gust) based upon damage with this tornado is 120 mph.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.

At approximately 5:30 pm an EF0 tornado touched down north of Yuba City and moved northeast, crossing from Sutter County into Yuba County and thereby north of Marysville.  There was little damage in the area that appeared to be caused by the tornado.  The determining factor was the credible description and sequence of events by witnesses who saw the tornado develop and move through peach and walnut groves.  There were no injuries nor fatalities.

Criteria is lower for the first storm of the season. Snow began at approximately midnight (PST) and increased to over 4 inches of snow by 7am (PST) at levels above 5000 ft. Snow levels were approximately 4500 ft, dropping to slightly below 4000 ft in local areas. Snowfall ended by early morning on October 23rd. Highest snow amounts at highest elevations were measured approximately 1-2 ft. Manzanita Lake (6000 ft) received approximately 5 of snow. Winds were 20-30 mph sustained with peak gusts over 50 mph at high elevation mountain passes.

Criteria is lower for the first storm of the season. Snow began at approximately midnight (PST) and increased to over 4 inches of snow by 5am (PST) at levels above 5000 ft. Snow levels had dropped to approximately 4000 ft in local areas. Snowfall ended by early morning on October 23rd. Highest snow amounts at highest elevations were measured approximately 2-3 ft. Blue Canyon (5280 ft) received 17, Boreal Ski Resort received 24-28, Kingvale (6200 ft) received approximately 27 total, and Sugar Bowl Ski Resort received 21-28 ft. Winds were 20-30 mph sustained with peak gusts over 50 mph at high elevation mountain passes. One fatality occurred: A 14-year old boy froze to death due to winter storm exposure after getting lost during a hunting trip. The body was found approximately 3 miles west of Hermit Valley Campground, Alpine County, which is approximately 8 miles west of Ebbett's Pass and 22 miles south of Lake Tahoe.

The Yuba City Tornado: Supercells developed behind the cold front along a north-south boundary in the middle of the Central Valley, where both instability and shear were large. The Sutter County Sheriff and Fire Department reported a tornado at approximately 2pm (PST), which was the first reported tornado of the day. The NWS storm survey team determined a touchdown at Mallard Lake Golf Center along Highway 99 just south of Yuba City. The tornado traveled northeast toward Oswald and Barry Roads and north along Railroad Ave. Estimated wind speeds were up to 100mph. The tornado snapped several trees at the golf course, damaged 30-40 small walnut and peach trees in a nearby orchard, lifted shingles on multiple homes, damaged a car port, blew down several fences, damaged several businesses, and lifted an outbuilding off its foundation and turned it upside down.

The Olivehurst Tornado: Supercells developed behind the cold front along a north-south boundary in the middle of the Central Valley, where both instability and shear were large. Emergency manager reported a tornado touchdown at approximately 2:30pm (PST). The estimated damage path length was a quarter mile with wind speeds estimated at 90-100mph. A sturdy roof on a wood frame building suffered significant damage. Metal roofs on several other industrial buildings were also badly damaged.

The Browns Valley Tornado: Supercells developed behind the cold front along a north-south boundary in the middle of the Central Valley, where both instability and shear were large. Law enforcement reported a brief tornado touchdown in a rice field. The estimated damage path length was about 100 ft to the northeast with wind speeds estimated at 70-80mph or less. No damage was associated with this tornado.

The Elk Grove Tornado: Supercells developed behind the cold front along a north-south boundary in the middle of the Central Valley, where both instability and shear were large. Reports of tornado damage were at approximately 3:45pm (PST) near Waterman and Grand Line Roads. The estimated damage path length was about a mile with wind speeds estimated at 90-100mph. A sturdy metal roof was bent back, tree trunks that were several feet in diameter were snapped. Dozens of houses were mildly damaged.

The Lake of the Pines Tornado: Supercells developed behind the cold front along a north-south boundary in the middle of the Central Valley, where both instability and shear were large. The Fire Department reported a tornado touchdown at approximately 4:30pm (PST). The estimated damage path length was approximately 4 miles with wind speeds estimated at 90-100mph. The tornado touched down near highway 49 and Combie Rd and snapped tree trunks of 1 to 3 ft in diameter. Many trees were uprooted and a few power lines were blown over. Some buildings were also badly damaged in the area.

Several hours of heavy rainfall from training storms caused local flooding in low-lying areas in Shasta County and parts of north Tehama County. Redding airport received approximately 1.75 inches of rain from 10am Nov. 20 to 10am Nov. 21st, but approximately 1.25 inches of that occurred from 2am-10am Nov 21st. Shasta Dam received approximately 3.50 to 4 inches of rain in that 24 hour period. The Corning area received approximately 0.37 inches. KRCR reported flash flooding at Hall Road along Thomes Creek where the creek rose significantly and flooded the low-lying area. At approximately 815am, a man from a vehicle had to be rescued by a CalFire helicopter as the car became mostly submerged in rushing water after driving across Hall Rd that was water-covered from the swollen creek water. The rushing water swept his vehicle. Other areas nearby were reported to have ponding of water on the roads.

Snow for this event began approximately 4pm on Saturday, November 17th through approximately 4pm Sunday, November 18th. Estimated snow amounts above 6000 ft were between 2-12 inches. North Fork American SNOTEL (6855 ft) reported about 11 inches of snow depth increase, but may be overestimated. West Walker Basin SNOTEL (9617 ft) reported over 9 inches of snow depth for that time period, although snow had begun accumulating prior to this event from a weaker system. South Fork American Basin (8353 ft) reported approximately 8-10 inches during this event. Soda Springs reported approximately 11 inches. Other snow amounts reported between 2-4 inches, which would not reach warning criteria.

A series of waves, associated with a warm atmospheric river event, came through Northern California and dropped several inches of snow for the Sierra Nevada mountains. Over 20 of snow was reported at Sierra at Tahoe (7000-8000 ft) on Nov 28-30, with a storm total of 38 for the whole event. Ebbetts Pass (8765 ft) received 25 on Nov 28-30, with a storm total of 30. Blue Lakes (8000 ft) received approximately 15 through Nov 30. CSS Lab (6855 ft) located along I-80 received approximately 7 through Nov 30. The largest accumulations of snowfall occurred Thursday into Friday, and again Saturday into Sunday (Dec 1-2). Winds were reported to gust up to 80-100+ mph at the highest elevations.

A series of waves, associated with a warm atmospheric river event, came through Northern California and dropped several inches of snow for the Sierra Nevada mountains. Snow began in the morning of Nov 28, and dropped about 27 inches of snow at Lower Lassen Peak between Nov 28-30. Additional snow fell with the event, bringing the Lassen storm total to about 39. The most intense 24 hour period occurred between Thursday and Friday with 15 at Lassen, which occurred during our winter storm warning. Winds were reported to gust up to 80-100+ mph at the highest elevations.

A series of storm waves, associated with a warm atmospheric river event, came through Northern California and dropped several inches of snow for the Sierra Nevada mountains. Over 20 of snow was reported at Sierra at Tahoe (7000-8000 ft) on Nov 28-30, with a storm total of 38 for the whole event. Ebbetts Pass (8765 ft) received 25 on Nov 28-30, with a storm total of 30 through Dec 2. Blue Lakes (8000 ft) received approximately 15 through Nov 30, with a couple more inches that fell through Dec 2. CSS Lab (6855 ft) located along I-80 received approximately 7 through Nov 30, and had a total of 12 as a storm total through Dec 2. The largest accumulations of snowfall occurred Thursday into Friday (Nov 29-30), and again Saturday into Sunday (Dec 1-2). Winds were reported to gust up to 80-100+ mph at the highest elevations.

A series of consecutive heavy rainfall events caused creeks and streams to rise rapidly due to ground saturation. Two to three feet of water was reported at the intersection of Highway 299 and Dry Creek Rd, as well as flooding farther northeast on Highway 299 from Montgomery Creek.

A series of consecutive heavy rainfall events caused creeks and streams to rise rapidly due to ground saturation. Reports of a trailer park flooded on Sunday due to rising creek levels along Arcade Creek. Winding Way (road) was reported as flooded in low lying areas as well.

A series of storm systems brought heavy rain and wind to northern California. In particular, winds increased overnight late Saturday night December 1st ahead of frontal rainband that moved through...and strong winds continued into Sunday morning December 2nd. A trained spotter reported multiple trees down, including one that fell onto a house that pierced two holes in his neighbor's roof. Another fallen tree in the area took out the siding of a garage nearby. Trees were down all throughout interior northern California from strong winds and saturated grounds, blocking roadways and taking out power lines. Winds in eastern Shasta County were estimated to gust up to 60-70 mph.

Several series of waves containing heavy rainfall hit northern California during a high impact atmospheric river event. The last series of waves that occurred Dec. 1st and Dec. 2nd dropped an additional 1-2 inches of rainfall in the motherlode region...on top of the 4-8 inches that had already fallen previously in the first series of waves. Grounds became overly saturated, which caused trees to collapse from saturated soils and heavy absorption of water. At approximately 8 am on Dec. 4th, one oak tree fell on a vehicle that was traveling 40 mph in a Ford F-150 pickup truck on westbound Green Valley Road, approaching Ponderosa Road, killing a 48 year old man after failing to avoid the falling oak tree. The other passenger in the back of the vehicle, a 10 year old boy, was unharmed.

Waves of precipitation entered northern California, bringing cold air and low snow levels. Trained spotters reported snow in the cities of Redding and Cottonwood at around 500-600 ft elevations, which is a rare event. Only light accumulations were reported...with the most being 3/4 to 1 in Redding.

A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing moderate to heavy snowfall. Snowfall began approximately mid-day on December 20th, and continued through mid-day December 23th. Stouts Meadow (near McCloud 12 ESE), elevation 5400 ft, received approximately 3.5 feet of snow during this time. Pit River locations, approximate elevations between 1500-2500 ft, received between 2-3 feet of snowfall. Locations at Sims, elevations approximately 1600-2500 ft, reported amounts between 1.5 to 2.5 feet of snowfall. Lower elevations such as Whiskeytown Reservoir, elevation approximately 1350 ft, reported approximately 3-5 inches of snow depth. One fatality occurred on Gregory Creek Road in Lakehead (noted by broadcast media), caused by a tree that had fallen on a trailer home from the weight of heavy snow and breezy winds. The victim, a male in his early 60s, was found the morning of Dec. 22, and the tree was approximately 2 feet in diameter.

A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing moderate to heavy snowfall. Snowfall began approximately during the afternoon on December 20th, and continued through mid-day December 23th. An observer in Burney, elevation approximately 3100 ft, reported a snow total of 34.5 inches. Fall River Mills, elevation approximately 3200 ft, reported about 2 feet of snow. Snow levels rose by December 22nd to above 2500-3000 ft, so snow amounts tapered off toward the end of the event.
