events.event_narrative: A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing moderate to heavy snowfall, with some breaks between snowfall amounts. Snowfall began approximately mid-day on December 20th, and continued through the evening December 23th. Snow levels rose to above 2500 ft on December 22nd, and above 3500 feet December 23rd. Alder springs, elevation 4555 ft, reported approximately 20-22 inches of snowfall during this time.

A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing moderate to heavy snowfall. Snowfall began in the morning hours of Dec 21st, and continued through the night of Dec. 23rd. Various ski resorts between 6500 ft to 8500 ft reported between 4 to 7 ft total of snowfall during this event. Majority of the ski resorts ranged between 4.5 and 5.5 ft. The highest values for these ski resorts were reported in Alpine, Nevada, and Placer Counties. Kingvale (6000 ft) received a storm total of 2 feet. Snow levels were overall above 3500 ft during the event for this zone. Two fatalities  resulted from avalanches at ski resorts on Dec. 24th (see Avalanche report).

A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing moderate to heavy snowfall. Snowfall began approximately the evening of December 20th, and continued through the evening of December 23rd. Spotters reported heavy snowfall beginning during the early hours of Dec 21st at Feather River Canyon (3200 ft), Meadow Valley (3800 ft), Greenville (3560 ft), and near Lake Almanor (4565 ft). Snow rates were 1 to 3 inches per hour for these locations. Lake Almanor/Chester area estimated about 3-3.5 ft of snowfall total. Lower Lassen Peak (8250 ft) received snow beginning as early as 6pm on Dec. 20th and reported over 5 ft (62 inches) of total snowfall during this event.

A series of waves passed through Northern California bringing snowfall that reached the lower elevations. Snowfall began approximately 6am on December 21st and continued through late morning December 21st for the Northern Sacramento Valley. A COOP spotter in Redding (500 ft) reported a snow accumulation of 1 inch on the ground. A spotter in Palo Cedro just east of Redding also reported accumulating snow on the ground in the morning. This event was significant since low elevation snow is rare in northern California. In addition, this winter episode caused winds to gust up to 55 mph in the Central Valley on Dec. 23rd, which caused an estimated 10k to 30k people to lose power.

events.cz_name: MOUNTAINS SOUTHWEST SHASTA COUNTY TO NORTHERN LAKE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: A band of precipitation came through the coastal and northern mountains beginning Christmas morning and ending the following morning. Rain amounts were between 0.25 to 1.00 inch. Snow data were unavailable for this zone. Snow estimates were approximately 6-8 for the storm total above 2500-3000 feet, which did not meet the warning criteria for the time period.

A band of heavy snow entered northwest Shasta County on Christmas morning and continued until the next morning. Snow levels were approximately above 2000 ft. Snow totals for Slate Creek (5700 ft) were approximately 11-12 inches and snow totals at Stouts Meadow (5400 ft) were approximately 7-10 inches. A spotter at Sims (approx 1600 ft) measured a storm total of 5 inches of new snow.

A band of heavy snow entered the Burney Basin area mid-day on Christmas, and continued through the next morning. Snow levels were above 2000 ft and snow fall total amount at Burney (3200 ft) was measured at 6 inches. Soldier Mountain (3700 ft) measured approximately 6 inches. These amounts did not reach warning criteria.

A wave of heavy snowfall passed through northern California beginning late Christmas morning and lingering showers ended the evening of Dec. 26th. Snow amounts on Lower Lassen Peak (8250 ft) were reported to be 10 inches, and mountain valley locations such as Quincy received up to 6 inches. A spotter in Twain (3200 ft; Feather River Canyon) received 4.5 inches of new snow. Warning criteria was not met.

A wave of heavy snowfall entered the Sierra mid-day on Christmas, and continued through the evening of Dec. 26th. Ebbett's Pass (8700 ft) reported 14 inches, CSS Lab (6850 ft) reported 16 inches, the spotter at Kingvale (6000 ft) reported 17.5 inches, and the spotter at Pacific House (approx. 3500 ft) reported 3 inches of new snow. Ski resorts reported significant snowfall amounts: Kirkwood Peak received 24 inches, Sierra at Tahoe received 12 inches, Soda Springs (6883 ft) received 28 inches, Boreal (7450 ft) received 16.5 inches, and Sugarbowl Peak received 30 inches.

A series of consecutive heavy rainfall events caused local flooding due to ground saturation and steep terrain. California Highway Patrol indicated that SR70 was closed from the Jarbo Gap area to Greenville along the Feather River due to extremely heavy rains and run off from the steep terrain. Damage was reported for the roadway and possibly to the bridge. Closure began at Big Bend Road on SR70 in area indicated.

A series of consecutive heavy rainfall events caused creeks and streams to rise rapidly due to ground saturation. A spotter reported flooding in the Butte Sink area along the Butte and Colusa County border. Approximately 4 inches of water has accumulated over the Gridley Rd-Colusa Hwy roadway, which has closed the road.

One fatality occurred when a male snowboarder, age 49, was caught in an avalanche at Donner Ski Ranch on Dec. 24th that occurred between 11am and noon. The man's body was found under 2-3 feet of snow at the base of the avalanche. The wind had blown snow to depths of 7 ft or more where the man was snowboarding.

A cold low pressure system moved through Feb. 18th and 19th. A strong precipitation band with low snow levels (1000-2000 ft) dropped a significant amount of snow in the Sierra foothills. Snowfall totals were reported as follows: Camino (3120 ft) received 7, Fiddletown (2500 ft) received 4, Soulsbyville (3000 ft) received 7, Nevada City (3000-3300 ft) received 7 to 8.5, San Andreas (1720 ft) received 4, Grass Valley (2422 ft) received 3, Placerville (2180 ft) received 6, Sonora (3000 ft) received 7, and Pine Grove (2100 ft) received 2. During the event, a 30-car pile up occurred on Highway 4 (Ebbetts Pass Highway) and Forest Meadows Drive. No known fatalities.

A cold low pressure system moved through the overnight hours of Feb 19th and continued through the evening of the 19th. A strong precipitation band with low snow levels (1000-2000 ft) dropped 6 to 12 inches at the ski resorts. Other spotters reported the following: Twain Harte (3,648 ft) received 8, Sugar Pine (4200 ft) received 8, Cedar Ridge (4050 ft) received 9.5, and Pacific House (3440 ft) received 6. Blue Canyon (5280 ft) received 10. During the event, a 50 to 100 car pile up occurred on Highway 49 and Rawhide Road near Tuttletown. No known fatalities.

The public reported a landspout tornado at approximately 1:30pm near Gerber, CA.  This tornado touched down in a farmland south of Worthington Ave. and tracked from northeast to southwest, hitting the east side of a large barn and destroying the roofing structure of the eastern side. The tornado scattered the metal roof shingles and wood pieces up to 200 ft away to both the northeast and southwest. Based on damage, the NWS tornado survey rated it as an EF0 with an estimation of 74 mph. Images and video confirmed that this tornado was a landspout.

A brief landspout tornado was reported by the public and verified as a landspout by video footage. This tornado was rated as an EF0 that occurred at approximately 2PM in a field south of Fairview Rd by Danley Rd. No damage and no injuries were associated with this tornado.

Snow began in the afternoon on March 5th and continued through the evening of March 6th, and reported to reach elevations locally down to 2000 ft. Stouts Meadow near McCloud (5400 ft) reported approximately 22 inches of snow received, and Slate Creek near Dunsmuir (5700 ft) reported approximately 20 inches of snow received. Peak winds gusted approximately between 30 and 50 mph for this area.

Snow began in the evening on March 5th and continued through the evening of March 6th, and reported to reach elevations locally down to 3000 ft. Lower Lassen Peak (8250 ft) reported 16 inches of snow accumulation, Harkness Flat near Chester (6200 ft) reported 9 inches of new snow, Rattlesnake near Greenville (6100 ft) reported 5 inches of new snow, and Snow Mountain near Burney (5950 ft) reported 13 inches of new snow. Reported peak winds gusted approximately between 30 and 40 mph for this area, with locally higher amounts for the ridge tops and higher elevations.

Snow began in the evening on March 5th and continued through the evening of March 6th, and reported to reach elevations locally down to 3000 ft. Kirkwood Ski resort (7800-9800 ft) reported 17-19 inches of snow, Sierra at Tahoe Resort reported 13 inches of snow, Soda Springs and Boreal Ski Resorts (7500 ft) reported 16 inches of snow, and Sugarbowl Ski Resort (6800-8300 ft) reported 11-16 inches of snow. Our Kingvale (6200 ft) spotter reported 16 inches of new snow, and Blue Canyon (5300 ft) automated sensor reported 10 inches of new snow. Reported peak winds gusted approximately between 30 and 50 mph for this area, with locally higher amounts for the ridge tops and higher elevations.

events.cz_name: MOUNTAINS SOUTHWEST SHASTA COUNTY TO NORTHERN LAKE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: Snow began in the afternoon on March 5th and continued through the evening of March 6th, and reported to reach elevations locally down to 2000-3000 ft. Eagle Peak (3700 ft) received between 5-6 inches of new snow, Alder Springs (4500 ft) received a few inches of new snow, and Saddle Camp (3850 ft) received approximately 6-7 inches of new snow. Snow amounts did not reach warning criteria.

Thunderstorms developed in Northern San Joaquin Valley and moved into the Southern Sacramento Valley and Motherlode. At approximately 1:00 AM PDT, a severe thunderstorm moved through Pioneer and dropped quarter size hail. A citizen reported the hail size and image to KCRA media.

Severe thunderstorms were slow-moving toward the north at 15 mph, and produced copious amounts of hail. One spotter reported hail drifts up to 3 ft along their yard fence. Hail was still there the following day.
Public reported a brief tornado with visible debris cloud in an empty field south of Shasta College. Tornado duration was approximately 2 minutes. This tornado was rated an EF0 with no known damage.

The Northern San Joaquin Valley experienced peak winds of 35-45 mph on Monday, April 8th. A tree fell in the road on March Ln. and Quail Lakes Dr. in Stockton, where peak winds reached 44 mph. Another large tree was ripped down on Kelly Ln. in Stockton. A tree fell down into the road in east Modesto, where winds peaked at around 37 mph. A 17-year-old student in Patterson was hit by a falling tree and suffered minor injuries.

The Southern Sacramento Valley experienced peak winds of 40-50 mph on Monday the 8th, and 35-40 mph on Tuesday the 9th. For Monday, a large tree limb fell on top of an SUV in Lincoln, CA and broke the wind shield of the vehicle. Several trees were reported down in midtown Sacramento, CA, where highest winds were reported to be 47 mph. At 9:30am on Monday, a lady reported a tree crashing through her bedroom ceiling on Campus Commons Drive in Sacramento, causing roof and window damage. For Tuesday, a large 20-year-old California Redwood tree fell onto the roof of a home on Mavis Avenue in Orangevale, CA.

A thunderstorm developed over the Sierra mountains near Downieville around 1:30 pm PDT and was reported to produce hail for over 30 minutes near Bucks Lake in Plumas County (between 3:20 pm PDT and 4:00 pm PDT). It became severe around 3:30 pm PDT with measured hail of 1 inch. The thunderstorm weakened after 4:00 pm PDT.

Redevelopment of thunderstorms that were producing torrential rainfall over the urban areas of Sacramento caused several instances of roadway flooding across the area. Law enforcement reported roadway flooding at Exposition Blvd and Heritage Lane with a vehicle stuck in the roadway, two vehicles stuck in water near Arden and Hwy 160, roadway flooding near Watt Ave and Marconi Ave, as well as roadway flooding at H Street and 37th Street.

Max temperatures in the Southern Sacramento Valley reached 100-107 degrees on Friday, and 105-110 degrees on Saturday. Minimum temperatures were approximately in the mid to upper 60s. The heat sickened at least 15 people, two critcally, at a morning graduation cermeony Saturday at Del Oro High School in Loomis, which forced the cancellation of the event and sent several people to the local hospitals. Many of those stricken suffered heat exhaustion and heat stroke and ranged in age from 15 to 80 years of age and older.

Max temperatures in the Central and Northern Sacramento Valley reached 102-111 degrees on Friday, and 103-112 degrees on Saturday. Minimum temperatures were quite warm, approximately in the low 70s to mid 80s.

Max temperatures in the Central and Northern Sacramento Valley reached 102-111 degrees on Friday, and 103-112 degrees on Saturday. Minimum temperatures were quite warm, approximately in the low 70s to mid 80s.
Max temperatures in the Northern San Joaquin Valley reached 100-106 degrees on Friday, and 106-110 degrees on Saturday. Minimum temperatures were approximately in the 60s.

An EF0 dust devil damaged the metal roof of a commercial building. The non-thunderstorm wind damage lasted a duration of approximately 5 minutes, at around 11:15-11:20 AM PDT on June, 19th. The damage included metal and wood roofing that was peeled backward, with some of the roofing landing on the adjacent ground.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 103 to 110 for the Southern Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to mid 70s overnight. High minimum and maximum temperature records were tied or broken for Sacramento Executive Airport and Downtown Sacramento during this period. The most significant record was that Downtown Sacramento tied an all-time record of 7 consectuve days of 105 degrees or higher for a maximum temperature. It tied with the record set for August 5th-11th, 1990.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 104 to 108 for the Northern San Joaquin Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to low 80s overnight. A max temperature record was broken for Stockton during this period.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 108 to 116 for the Northern Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between upper 60s to 90, with majority in the 70s, overnight. Max temperature records were broken for Redding and Red Bluff during this period.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 101 to 109 for the Central Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to low 80s overnight. A max temperature record was broken for Marysville during this period.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 103 to 110 for the Southern Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to mid 70s overnight. High minimum and maximum temperature records were tied or broken for Sacramento Executive Airport and Downtown Sacramento during this period. The most significant record was that Downtown Sacramento tied an all-time record of 7 consectuve days of 105 degrees or higher for a maximum temperature. It tied with the record set for August 5th-11th, 1990.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 108 to 116 for the Northern Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between upper 60s to 90, with majority in the 70s, overnight. Max temperature records were broken for Redding and Red Bluff during this period.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 101 to 109 for the Central Sacramento Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to low 80s overnight. A max temperature record was broken for Marysville during this period.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 104 to 108 for the Northern San Joaquin Valley for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to low 80s overnight. A max temperature record was broken for Stockton during this period. One fatality in Ceres, CA: 77-year old man died from heat-related complications on July 2nd.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 95 to 108 for the Delta for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to mid 70s overnight. The delta breeze had been minimal, so cooling relief was also minimal.

Thunderstorms developed in the afternoon along the Sierra Nevada crest and spread eastward. Witnesses reported a 66-year old female died in a campground after a lightning strike hit the area. No enter/exit woulds reported to confirm a direct hit.  However, evidence would suggest cardiac arrest due to a lightning strike was likely the cause of death.
Strong thunderstorm passed over Fall River Mills in the evening, which produced large hail of 1.75 diameter.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused a rock slide along Highway 70 on mile post 33.03 near Paxton, CA. The rock slide occurred around 6:47 pm PDT on July 2nd, where two large boulders were pushed onto the road. This rockslide caused delays to travelers, and CalTrans was called out to remove the boulders.

High temperatures ranged from approximately 95 to 108 for the Delta for 7 consecutive days. Minimum temperatures ranged between mid 60s to mid 70s overnight. The delta breeze had been minimal, so cooling relief was also minimal.

Strong thunderstorms developed along the Sierra and southern Cascades. One thunderstorm, in particular, strengthened over Lassen National Park. As this storm slowly moved north over the area, it dropped a lot of 1 inch hail and heavy rain. This was reported by a park ranger located at the park entrance near Manzanita Lake.

The Rim Fire was a wildfire that started on August 17th at around 3:15pm PDT in Tuolumne County. It was located in the Groveland Range District of Stanislaus National Forest. The fire grew to be the 3rd largest wildfire in California's history, at 257,314 acres. For the TOTAL FIRE EVENT: It cost approximately $127.2 million, caused 10 injuries, burned 11 residences, 3 commercial properties, and 98 outbuildings. For the month of AUGUST ONLY: 222,777 acres, $60 million, 5 injuries, 11 residences, 3 commercial properties, and 97 outbuildings.

The Rim Fire was a wildfire that started on August 17th at around 3:15pm PDT in Tuolumne County. It was located in the Groveland Range District of Stanislaus National Forest. The fire grew to be the 3rd largest wildfire in California's history, at 257,314 acres. For the TOTAL FIRE EVENT: It cost approximately $127.2 million, caused 10 injuries, burned 11 residences, 3 commercial properties, and 98 outbuildings. For the month of SEPTEMBER ONLY: 34,358 more acres, additional $65.8 million, 5 additional injuries, 0 new residences, 0 new commercial properties, and 1 new outbuildings.

The Clover Fire developed in the community of Igo, 10 miles southwest of Redding, and forced many people to evacuate their homes. The fire grew to 8,073 acres, killed one 56-year old male who chose not to evacuate his home, and injured six people. The fire destroyed 68 residences and 128 outbuildings, and it damaged 5 additional residences and 10 outbuildings. Cost of the fire is unknown.

The Rim Fire was a wildfire that started on August 17th at around 3:15pm PDT in Tuolumne County. It was located in the Groveland Range District of Stanislaus National Forest. The fire grew to be the 3rd largest wildfire in California's history, at 257,314 acres. For the TOTAL FIRE EVENT: It cost approximately $127.2 million, caused 10 injuries, burned 11 residences, 3 commercial properties, and 98 outbuildings. For the month of OCTOBER ONLY: approximately 179 more acres, additional $1.4 million, 0 additional injuries, 0 new residences, 0 new commercial properties, and 0 new outbuildings.

Showers developed in a southwest to northeast line from southwest of Stockton area to northeast of Quincy. Trained spotters reported 1.50 of heavy rainfall as convective showers trained over the area all day long on Sept 2nd. Flooding was reported at 10:43 am PST along Highway 49 in Alta Sierra. Flooding was also reported at 10:46 am PST along Highways 49 and 20 in Nevada City. Rain continued through the early morning Sept. 3rd.

North wind event produced sustained winds of 15 to 25mph with gusts up to 35 to 45mph for the Southern Sacramento Valley. The power went out for nearly 11,000 customers in Rio Linda and North Highland (northern Sacramento) areas. Additional several hundred power outages were recorded in West Sacramento, Orangevale, and Fair Oaks. Total power outages in the Sacramento metro were estimated to be 16,000 customers due to strong winds. Two of the outages were said to be caused by falling tree limbs.

Onshore winds increased in the afternoon Oct. 27th ahead of the strong trough. Winds in Tracy measured 44mph, Stockton measured 44mph, and Campo Seco measured 49mph. Blowing dust greatly restricted visibility and brought traffic to a slow crawl on highly traveled roads (I-5 and I-580) in the late afternoon and evening hours. The California Highway Patrol reported that six big rigs on I-580 were knocked over between 6pm PDT Sunday to 5am PDT Monday. Two drivers suffered minor to moderate injuries.

Strong onshore winds brought down large trees for the Southern Sacramento Valley. Sacramento Executive AP peaked at 41mph, Sacramento International AP peaked at 46mph, and Vacaville/Nut Tree peaked at 36mph. Broadcast media reported several large trees down in Sacramento which hit houses, powerlines, and cars. A tree fell on a home near Sac State that caused significant roof damage.

The low pressure system brought the first significant snows of the winter season. The  snow was confined to the higher terrain  (mainly above 6500 ft), but did impact Interstate 80 and Donner Pass. Snow amounts reported by spotters include 9 at Kingvale, 14 at Soda Springs, 15 at Sugarbowl Peak, 12 at Sugarbowl base, 8.9 at Forni Ridge, 11.6 at 5 ENE of Kyburz, and 5.8 at 5 ENE Pinecrest.

Strong wind gusts of 50 to 80 mph were measured over South Lake County. Cow Mountain Ridge (3355ft) reported 78mph, whereas lower elevations reported 50-65mph. Damage reports consisted of several powerlines down, trees down onto cars, an RV park, and houses, thousands of power outages, and damage to two barns and fences. Largest damage areas were reported around Clearlake, Nice, and Upper Lake.

Strong wind gusts of 50 to 75 mph were estimated and measured over the Motherlode. Several trees were down, including trees in the American Fire area. Thousands of power outages were reported. A 52 year old female car passenger was killed by a 30 inch diameter portion of a dead tree that broke off partway up its trunk. This portion fell on the car killing the passenger and injuring the drive. The incident happened at approximately 8am on 11/21, located 2 miles west-southwest of Dobbins in Yuba County. Officials presumed winds may have factored into the incident. In addition, the high winds caused significant damage to the South Yuba Canal in the Bear Valley area east of Nevada City, cutting water flows from the mountains into the Grass Valley-Nevada City area, as reported by PG&E and Nevada Irrigation District (NID). The damage was widespread, with numerous large trees falling into and over the canal, breaking and collapsing flumes. The damage occurred in several sections of the 19-mile waterway which extends from lake Spaulding to the Scott Flat Lake area.

Strong wind gusts of 70 to 90 mph were estimated or measured over far northern Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades region. A location 12 miles west of Caribou in Plumas County measured 86mph from the Mesonet, and a location 7 miles east-northeast of Mill Creek (6730ft) in Plumas County reported 87mph. Multiple trees were reported down, including multiple powerlines down and power outages. There was a report that strong winds blew a moving van off the road and into the Feather River, 1 mile northeast of Pulga in Butte County sometime during the event. The driver was injured and hospitalized with hypothermia, according to the Forest Service.

Strong wind gusts of 60 to 90 mph were measured over the northern Sierra Nevada. A location 6 miles north-northwest of Downieville in Sierra County measured 88mph, and a location 11 miles south-southeast of Cisco (7100ft) in Placer County reported 90mph. Reports of several trees and limbs down, blocking roadways including Highways 49 and 50. There was a report of a tree falling on a powerline and starting a fire 4 miles northeast of Glencoe in Calaveras County. There was also a report of a rockslide 1 mile west-northwest of Strawberry in Tuolumne County that made a local road impassable. Local media reported 3 homes were damaged in Kyburz in El Dorado County. In addition, the high winds caused significant damage to the South Yuba Canal in the Bear Valley area east of Nevada City, cutting water flows from the mountains into the Grass Valley-Nevada City area, as reported by PG&E and Nevada Irrigation District (NID). The damage was widespread, with numerous large trees falling into and over the canal, breaking and collapsing flumes. The damage occurred in several sections of the 19-mile waterway which extends from lake Spaulding to the Scott Flat Lake area.

A cold storm system spread precipitation across northwest Shasta County for several hours. The low snow levels associated with this system resulted in snow to locations that do not normally receive accumulating snow. There were 3 inches of snow at Shasta Dam, 6-8 inches in the foothills including Sims, and up to 8-12 inches for the higher peak elevations. I-5 was closed for a period of time due to the wintery conditions and multiple car accidents.

The cold, low elevation snow system brought several inches of snow to the valley floor, which is rare for the area. Areas in Redding and Anderson (400-700ft elevations) received 4-6 inches of snow, with 1-2 inches farther south near Red Bluff and Cottonwood (300-500ft elevations). Locations near Dairyville also received 1-2 inches of snow.  Spotters reported non accumulating snow at elevations as low as 200ft.

The cold, low elevation snow system brought 4 to 12 inches of snow to the foothills. Shingletown received 5-8 inches of snow, and near Brush Creek received 12 inches. Magalia received around 7 inches.

The cold, low elevation snow system brought snow to western Plumas and Lassen Park area for several hours. The slopes received approximately 6 to 10 inches of snow, with highest amounts over the Lassen Peak region (18-22). Quincy and Chester received 4-6 inches of snow along the east side of the crest.

The cold, low elevation snow system brought significant amounts to the motherlode foothills, with elevations as low as approximately 800 ft. Auburn (1000 ft elevation) received 1 inch of snow. Grass Valley and Nevada City area received anywhere from 4 to 8 inches, reported by spotters. Higher amounts were reported by spotters near Groveland (12) and Sonora (10). Placerville, Camino, and Somerset areas along and near Highway 50 received 5 to 8 inches. In addition to the snow, the very cold temperatures prompted Nevada and Tuolumne counties to open warming centers in Grass Valley and Sonora, respectively, for several days.

The cold, low elevation snow system dumped significant amounts of snow along the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada. Kirkwood ski resort reported 24-32 inches of snow along their slopes. Other ski resorts such as Sugarbowl and Sierra at Tahoe reported 18-22 inches. Near Donner Pass, areas received 18-22 inches of snow. Kingvale spotter reported 23 inches. Lower elevations such as Sonora (3500-4000ft elevations) reported 12-14 inches, Pacific House (3500ft) reported 11 inches, and Pollock Pines (3900ft) reported 6-8 inches. |In addition, due to multiple spinout accidents on I-80 during the event, Caltrans temporarily closed I-80 eastbound at Applegate (2000ft) and I-80 westbound at the stateline for approximately an hour (early morning on December 7th).

The cold, low elevation snow system only brought around 4 inches to the city of Burney, with locally higher amounts for the higher elevations, as the system spread from northwest to southeast across interior northern California.

events.cz_name: MOUNTAINS SOUTHWEST SHASTA COUNTY TO NORTHERN LAKE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The cold, low elevation snow system only brought around 4 inches for Alder Springs, with less amounts at lower elevations. Some of the higher peaks in northern Lake County were estimated to receive 6-8 inches, but no datasets were found to verify.

A plethora of records were set across interior northern California for January. The following is from one of our oldest record sites, Downtown Sacramento. The highlights include: the longest dry period (52 days) during the rainy season from Dec. 8th, 2013 to Jan. 28th, 2014 that did not receive measurable rainfall, the third driest January in history since 1950 with 0.20 inches of rainfall which is only 5% of normal, highest January average maximum temperature of 66.1 degrees, new all-time record high for the month of January set on Jan. 24th of 79 degrees, broke the number of days with high temperatures of 70 degrees or higher with 3 days, record high temperatures were set on 12 different days, and lastly, everyday of January 2014 had a daytime high temperature that was above normal for the month for Downtown Sacramento.

A Pacific storm brought snowfall to the Sierra Nevada Wednesday morning through Friday morning. By Thursday morning, ski resorts (7000-8500 ft elevation) reported 4 to 6 inches of snow, with locally higher amounts on their peaks up to 8 inches. By Friday morning, the ski resorts reported 8 to 16 inches of snow from the entire storm total.

A Pacific storm brought snow Friday and Friday night for northwest Shasta County mountains. Slate Creek near Dunsmuir (5700ft) reported a storm total of approximately 12 inches when snow levels were around 3000-4000 ft Friday. The area received 1-4 inches of liquid equivalent.

A Pacific storm brought snow Friday and Friday night for Southern Cascade/Northern Sierra mountains. Harkness Flat near Chester (6200ft) reported a storm total of approximately 14 inches when snow levels were around 3500-4500 ft Friday. Some higher locations were estimated to receive over 2-3 ft of snow Friday. The area received 2-4 inches of liquid equivalent.

A Pacific storm brought snow Friday and Friday night for the northern Sierra Nevada. Blue Canyon (5200ft) reported a storm total of approximately 14 inches when snow levels were around 3500-4500 ft Friday. Kingvale (6200ft) reported a storm total of 20 inches. The ski resorts (8000-9000ft) reported 1 to 1.5ft of storm total snow. The area received 2-4 inches of liquid equivalent.

The third Pacific storm wave was semi-connected to the second wave and began mid day Feb 8, but lasted through early Feb 10. Snow levels started off around 5000-6000 ft Saturday but rose to over 7000 ft by Monday. This wave brought 2-4 of liquid equivalent for the Sierra, which equated to an additional 1-2.5 ft of snow above 6500ft. Carson's Pass (8350ft) reported 29 of snow total mid-day Saturday through early Monday, and Ebbett's Pass (8760ft) reported 31 of snow total and Echo Peak (7670ft) reported 36 of snow during that time.  Ski resorts reported an additional 1-2 ft of snow.

The first wave of Pacific storms started Wednesday evening, Feb. 5, and continued through Thursday afternoon, Feb. 6th. This wave only brought approximately 4-8 inches to the western slope of the Sierra. Majority of ski resorts and SNOTELs reported 4-6 inches above 7000ft, and Blue Canyon received approximately 4 inches at 5200ft. Local news reported a fatal accident on I-80 near Soda Springs. A woman was killed by a car spinning out of control from the wintry weather at approximately 5:40pm, which struck her and she was thrown 80-100 ft. She and her driver were standing outside on the shoulder at the time, due to their own car spinning out a short time earlier.

A heavy band of rain moved through Chico approximately 10pm on Sunday, Feb. 9th, through past midnight. The city of Chico received approximately 0.80 inches in 30-40 minutes, and approximately 1.00 inch in an hour, with additional heavy rainfall on the foothills to the east. A new subdivision that was under construction had pour drainage causing occupied homes to flood, particularly on Bancroft Drive. The houses that reported significant damage were addresses 2855, 2857, 2859, 2861, and 2863 on Bancroft Drive located near East 20th St, just east of Bruce Road. A wall of water came from the foothills to the east that overwhelmed the drains filling up the surrounding area, and rose as high as 2 ft into some of the homes causing significant damage. Note: the area selected includes the significantly damaged homes, but reports of flooded streets extended through many of the subdivisions in the area with no damage reported.

The first storm that moved through was slightly warmer and stronger than the second storm, bringing snow to elevations mainly above 6000ft. Blue Canyon (5200ft) reported 2, Kingvale (6200ft) reported 4, and Echo Peak (7670ft) reported 7. Kirkwood ski resort (above 7500ft) reported 13-16, Carson Pass received approximately 15 to 17, and Sierra at Tahoe ski resort (above 7000ft) reported 10. Donner Summit (7200ft) received 9 while Sugarbowl ski resort (above 6500ft) had 6 to 12.
The second storm wave that went through on Friday produced 5 of snow at Blue Canyon (5200ft), 6 at Soda Springs (7000ft), 9 at Donner Peak (8383ft), and around 10 to 14 at Carson Pass (8353ft).

A member of the public witnessed and video recorded a tornado over Conaway Ranch just southeast of Woodland (Yolo County) at approximately 6:17 to 6:22pm Friday evening, February 28th. He reported observing the tornado touch down near County Roads 103 and 25, and traveled north-northeast for about 100 yards. It then lifted back to a funnel cloud for about 400-500 yards before touching back down in a flooded rice field. It traveled for another 100 yards near the levee before lifting. No visible damage observed, and the tornado was rated an EF0.

Northeasterly to easterly winds were gusting over the Motherlode area Tuesday afternoon into Wednesday afternoon. Wind gusts were reported to be 30-40 mph across the zone. California Highway Patrol reported that a large pine tree fell down on top of a car along Mother Lode Drive located 2 miles NW of Diamond Springs early Wednesday morning, trapping two people inside the vehicle. The crash blocked both lanes of Mother Lode Drive for several hours. No injuries were reported.

Northerly wind gusts up to 35 to 45 mph brought trees down across the delta area Tuesday and Wednesday. Regions near Vallejo gusted up to around 35 mph. California Highway Patrol reported that a downed tree on power wires caused a fire near the intersection of Hargus Avenue and Banning Way in Vallejo early Wednesday morning. No injuries were reported.

A dust devil developed on the property near an old tin roofed barn. As the dust devil encountered the barn, a large section of the tin roof was ripped off and the pieces were thrown several hundred feet into the air. A neighbor reported that one of the pieces was found almost a mile down the road. The individual tin sections were about 6 feet long and 2 feet wide. Approximately 35-40 tin panels were ripped off the barn. The dust devil lasted for around 2 minutes.

An EF0 tornado touched down near Highway 99 between Skyway Road and Neal Road at around 7:15pm PDT. Winds were estimated to be 65mph. A rotted tree along Neal Road was blown down, and branches were blown off of surrounding trees. Swirl marks were on the ground, but the tornado was no more than 10-15 yards wide.

Based on eye witness interviews we believe this was the first tornado to touch down around 5:30 pm, and then tracked southeast for about 5-10 minutes. A pheasant pen and an outbuilding both lost their roofs.  The outbuildings roof was made of sheet metal and some individual pieces were thrown between 800-1000 feet east/southeast of the outbuildings location. Some of the heavier pieces (150 lbs) were thrown 350 feet from the original outbuilding.

Based on eye witness interviews, believe this tornado originated around 5:30pm as well and tracked nearly due east along CR41. It removed the roof of a barn near Road R, damaged an outbuilding made of sheet metal, turned over a carport and broke a utility pole (8 inches in diameter) of a local residence just west of Road S.  An outcrop of cottonwood trees on a dairy farm at CR 41 and TT was badly damaged. Some of the tree limbs landed on structures to house calves, but no livestock were injured. Also, down road TT, a stop sign was ripped off its metal pole and thrown 50 yards in the field just east.

Based on eye witness interviews, this tornado originated around 5:45 pm at a residence along CR 39, west of Road P. Based on damage, the tornado appeared to track along the fence of the residence, taking out deciduous trees before turning west and taking out the chain link fence. It threw lawn furniture into the residences pool, and lifted an awning up. Two support beams under the awning were pushed over before the awning was returned to it���s original location resting on the remaining support beams. The tornado then tracked through some orange trees, relieving them of a majority of their fruit, then another row of deciduous trees, pushing them to the west. The tornado then tracked through their almond tree orchard uprooting or breaking 60+ of their trees and removing almonds from other trees. The tornado tracked west to the next resident���s orchard taking out another dozen or so of his trees, but a majority of the crop was stripped off the trees. It then hit a tractor parked near his orchard, removing the shade shield and throwing it 157 feet. (Weight is 90 lbs). It also damaged a large eucalyptus tree with a large portion of the tree falling in between the residence and an outbuilding, with a portion landing on a dog kennel just below the tree. 2 trucks on the premises had a back and passenger rear window blown out by flying debris or hail. One of the tucks also sustained damage to a metal tool box in back of the truck. A debris path was apparent across CR 39 as it moved south of the road and impacted another almond orchard.  Not much damage to north end of orchard, so tornado may have lifted up for a bit. Tornado touched back down just behind the residence and uprooted/broke 30+ trees. A cotton wood tree on the east end of the residence, top 1/3 of the tree was broken off, and landed immediately to the west into an alfalfa field. Toward the end of the row of almond trees near the residence, one of the uprooted trees was thrown 227 yards WSW into the alfalfa field. There was also a 24 foot debris path across the gravel road where the tree was dragged/carried into the field.

EF0 tornado began in the field just southwest of Roseville, but did not cause damage until it reached the Pleasant Grove Blvd housing developments in West Roseville. The tornado winds were estimated to be 75-85mph. Several windows were blown out amongst the houses, 25-30 feet of fence was blown down, projectile damage was found to stucco. The tornado lasted approximately 5-10 minutes.

An EF0 tornado touched down in a field just south of Nicolaus at approximately 5:17pm and lasted a duration of a couple minutes. No damage was reported from the tornado besides swirl marks on the ground.

At approximately 7:40pm, a trained spotter saw a funnel cloud associated with a supercell near Nord, CA while travelling on Highway 99 just east of Cana Highway. He witnessed the funnel cloud briefly touch down to the ground and then lift again. NWS storm survey found an uprooted tree in an orchard where the touchdown occurred, and swirl marks in the ground surrounding the tree. No injuries were reported.

The Rim Fire burn scar area received 0.20 to over 1 of rainfall from thunderstorms on the early morning of March 6th. The ground was previously saturated due to rainfall for several days prior to this event. There were approximately 10-11 different debris flow slides along the roadway. The cost of the road repair (removal of slide material, limited necessary reconstruction of road prism and culvert function, and storm proofing) was approximately $50,000 in direct engineering contracting costs. The road had just been rebuilt to new standards prior to the slides. No loss of tree productivity costs because the slopes above and below the road were non-commercial stands.

A series of snow showers brought heavy snow amounts to the Northern Sierra Nevada, where the heaviest snow fell between March 26 and into March 27th. Ski resorts reported 10-15 inches of new snow in 24 hours. SNOTEL CSS Lab site at 6855 ft reported 14 inches. Blue Canyon at 5280 ft reported 8 inches during this period. Kingvale spotter around 6200 ft received 11 inches.

A series of snow showers brought snow to far northern Sierra Nevada/Western Plumas County area. Harkness Flat near Chester (6200 ft) reported approximately 8 inches of snow was received between March 26th and 27th. Other sites reported between 4-6 inches or less of snow.

Snow levels dropped down to around 3500 ft for the Northern Sierra Nevada on March 29th. Blue Canyon received 11 inches of snow between 4pm PDT the 29th and 4am PDT the 30th. Sugarbowl Ski Resort reported 23-30 inches of new snow from the 24 hour period March 29-30. Kingvale spotter (6200 ft) reported 17 inches of new snow.

Snow levels dropped down near 3000 ft for the far Northern Sierra Nevada/Western Plumas County area on March 29th. Harkness Flat near Chester (6200 ft) received about 14 inches of new snow. Lassen Lodge (4200 ft) received approximately 20 inches of new snow.

A cold Pacific storm entered interior California and brought heavy snow to the Sierra Nevada. Blue Canyon (5200 ft) received 19 inches of new snow from March 31 to April 1. Ebbett's Pass (8765 ft) received approximately 10 inches of new snow. Kingvale spotter (6200 ft) received a total of 18 inches. Pacific House (3400 ft) reported about 4 inches.

A few inches of snow fell over far Northern Sierra Nevada as a cold Pacific storm moved through the area March 31st through April 1st. Lassen Lodge (4200 ft) received around 6 inches of new snow, and Harkness Flat (6200 ft) received around 4 inches of new snow.

During a wet/rainy day, breezy winds occurred on March 29th for the Southern Sacramento Valley, where winds gusted up to around 20 mph. A driver of a sedan was killed and the passenger was injured after a large oak tree fell on their vehicle. The event occurred around 12:20pm on Sunrise Blvd near Highland Ave in Citrus Heights, CA. Another driver in a minivan was injured after hitting the downed tree and striking a utility pole.

A strong late season storm brought heavy snow Thursday night through Friday night. Snowfall amounts reached warning criteria level, with Donner Pass receiving 18, Blue Canyon (5280ft) receiving 13, Kingvale (6200ft) receiving 18, Ebbetts Pass (8765ft) receiving 16, and Soda Springs over 15. Kingvale reached criteria as early as Friday morning, while Blue Canyon did not reach criteria until Friday afternoon.

The Sand Fire began east of Highway 49, 5 miles north of Plymouth (south of Placerville) on the afternoon of July 25th. The fire was caused by a vehicle driving into dry vegetation, and was considered a CalFire incident. The fire burned in both Amador and El Dorado Counties, reaching 4,240 acres by the time it was 100% contained on August 2nd. It burned 20 residences, and 47 outbuildings, and there were 2 injuries reported with the fire.

events.cz_name: MOUNTAINS SOUTHWEST SHASTA COUNTY TO NORTHERN LAKE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The Bully Fire in Shasta County began on the afternoon of July 11th as weather conditions were becoming drier and warmer. The fire started near Plantina Road at Bland Road west of Igo and Ono communities, caused by a vehicle driving over dry vegetation. By the time it was contained, the fire grew 12,661 acres, destroyed 20 structures, injured 21 people, and resulted in 1 death. The fire was estimated to have resulted in approximately 20 million dollars in damage and fire suppression efforts.

A wildfire broke out in the town of Collinsville around 2pm on July 4th, which destroyed 8 homes, damaged 3 more homes, burned boats and vehicles. The fire displaced 25 residents and caused an estimated 2.5 million dollars in damage. The cause of the fire was unknown, though the dry and windy conditions (20-25mph gusts) along with 4th of July celebrations may have been a factor.
A strong thunderstorm produced quarter size hail. The ground was covered with 2 inches of hail.
Rocks and mud slides on Highway 36 near Wildwood and Harrison Gulch roads due to torrential rain. Water was flowing on roads, along with accumulating hail.
Rocks on Highway 36 near Wildwood due to heavy rain. The roadway was flooded.

Stream bank erosion, with some scouring, rilling, and sheet erosion. Sediment deposited in creek bed at multiple road/creek crossings. There was also float-able debris that was later removed. Road was over-topped at multiple locations. Estimated Granite Creek Basin flow of 1200 CFS, a very high amount for the basin. Flash flood duration of 2 hours and 30 minutes.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain over Rim Fire Burn scar. Storm total of 1.31 inches in 2 hours, heavy rain for 30 minutes.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain over Rim Fire Burn scar. Storm total of 1.69 in, for approximately 2 hours.
Heavy rain fell on the west shore of Lake Almanor. Road flooding on state Highway 89 on the west side of the lake.
A trained spotter reported quarter size hail near Burney.
A firefighter reported golf ball size hail at the Eiler Fire.
Quarter-size hail was reported on the se flank of the Eiler Fire.

A 19 year old man and a 19-year-old women were driving in a vehicle that was swept off a small bridge over Lack Creek. Both were found drowned, their car about three quarters of a mile down stream. About 3.12 inches of rain fell nearby, measured by a RAWS station at Shingletown over 24 hours.  Of that, 2.87 inches of rain fell in the 5 hours before the accident.

A large fire whirl created a 2 mile damage path, documented by Forest Service personnel, resulted in damage equivalent to an EF-0 EF-1 tornado. Whole large trees were pulled up out of the ground, the bark stripped off cedar trees, metal tightly wrapped around logs/poles, and a culvert pulled up that had been buried under dirt.||Radar signatures that day indicated there were no storms near the fire.  The only radar signatures were of the smoke plume around the time of the fire whirl (between 1:30-3:30 PDT).

The King Fire destroyed 12 residences and 68 other buildings. There were 10 firefighters injured, and 97,099 acres burned by the end of the month. Hundreds of residents were evacuated. The fire was caused by arson and was estimated to have cost more than 90 million dollars for fire suppression efforts.
Rockville Rd. flooded, with erosion to the road and rocks from a wall on the road.

Rains produced several small debris flows. One was on Forebay Road after it crosses the American River and becomes Forest Road 123N34 due to storm rains.|A second debris flow deposit was recorded at the Day Use area at Forbear Road and the South Fork American River. Some minor mudflow deposits occurred below the denuded slope of the upper burned portion of Spring Valley Road.
Heavy rain from several days of thunderstorms caused debris flows, blocking the road to Brush Creek Reservoir.
CHP reported roadway flooding near Panorama Pt. Rd. and Balls Ferry Rd.
Hail up to quarter size.
Winds gusted to 60 mph.

There was 5 inches of new snow reported at Kingvale 6100 feet and at Soda Springs 6700 feet, along with gusty winds.  Chain controls were required, and traffic slow downs were reported on Interstate 80.

A single engine plane (Cessna 172) crashed on a remote hillside between Gopher Flat Road and Amador Road, just north of Sutter Creek, in Amador County, CA. There were 2 adult male fatalities. The plane was flying from Gilroy, CA to Sutter Creek, CA. Foggy conditions were present at Auburn Airport to the north, between 11:55 PST and 13:15 PST. Reduced visibility down to around 2 miles was recorded at Columbia Airport to the south at 11:35 PST. The exact time of the crash is currently unknown, but Amador County deputies received reports of the downed plane just after noon.

A cold front brought strong winds. A tree fell on a vehicle on Elliot Road in the city of Paradise at 7:48 am. This caused an adult female fatality. Elliott Road was closed from Ingalls Road to Copeland Road for a time, while crews responded to the scene.
Northeast winds behind a cold front brought down large trees in Paradise, Butte County. At 7:19 am PST, 2 large trees fell on a residence on Lofty Lane, which resulted in the death of an adult male.

A cold system brought light snow as low as 4100 feet (Kyburz), with accumulating snow above 5000 feet. Five inches of snowfall was reported at Kingvale at 6100 feet. This brought traffic slowdowns on I-80 and Highway 50.

Snowfall amounts near 6000 feet were around 6 inches, with up to a foot at Donner Summit at 7200 feet. The slippery roads caused travel difficulties and delays over Sierra passes, aggravated by increased traffic due to the holiday weekend.

A 2 vehicle car crash occurred on Highway 4 off Van Allen Rd., east of the city of Stockton, resulting in 5 fatalities and 3 injuries. The accident occurred at approximately 6:30 am PST and is thought to be related to poor visibility from fog. First responders reported visibility less than 100 feet when they arrived on scene. Visibility at Stockton Municipal Airport, which is about 10 miles west, was measured at a quarter mile at 6 and 7 am PST.

A 2 vehicle car crash occurred on on Highway 4 near Stockton St. and Charter Way in the city of Stockton, resulting in a fatality. A pickup truck struck a big rig which was pulling onto the highway. The pickup truck then struck a utility pole, with the driver later pronounced dead at the scene. The accident occurred at approximately 4:30 am PST and is thought to be related to poor visibility from fog. Visibility at Stockton Municipal Airport was measured at a quarter mile from 4 pm the previous day through 1 pm that afternoon.
Boulder Creek over topped banks and flooded Premier RV Resort.
There were 3 inches of standing water in backyard, with sandbags used to protect home. Heavy rain lasted about 12 hours.
Flash flooding caused a hard closure of Highway 36 at Baker Road.
Tehama County Sheriff's Office reported flooding of roads at multiple locations. Received a report of up to 6 feet of water flowing over a road. Closed a stretch of Highway 36.
Mudslide reported near the intersection of Baker Rd. and Monrovia.
Flooding reported at intersection of Jellys Ferry Dr. and Oakwood.

There was flooding and impacts along Highway 99 from numerous creeks overtopping their banks in addition to earthen berm or earthen levee failures. There were issues on the following creeks: |    Salt Creek (Overtopped at Highway 99 and Highway 36 location)|    Antelope Creek (Private earthen berm failure at Rancho Ave))|    Craig Creek (Overtopped near Craig Road and Rancho Ave)|    Dye Creek (Over topped and earthen berm failure between Shasta blvd and 62nd Ave)|Highway 99 was closed from highway 36 to Aramayo Way for many hours (Wednesday evening through early Thursday morning) until the water receded and things could be cleaned up. There were 213 homes impacted from the flooding, with significant damage from water and mud. Many homes had several feet of water. Fields and orchards were also flooded.|Damage to homes, bridges, fencing, crops, and beehives totaled $2.5 million. Repairs and remediation to the berms totaled $4.25 million.
Flooding at Auburn Folsom Rd. and Douglas Blvd. Two vehicles stalled in flood.
Roadway flooding at Foresthill Rd. off ramp in North Auburn. No vehicle could pass.
Grass Valley Rd. and Atwood Rd. 2 Vehicles stuck.
I80 and Clipper Gap Rd. Lane 1 had 1-2 feet deep water, 75 feet across, flooding the entire off ramp.
There were 10-12 homes flooded in Granite Bay.
Road closed at Country Club and Eureka, with vehicles stuck at the location.
Watt Ave. and Roseville Rd. number 1 lane flooded with 2 feet of water due to clogged drain.
I-80 at Watt Ave. Eastbound Underpass had significant flooding due to heavy rain and pump failure. This resulted in major traffic backup, lasting several hours during evening rush hour.
Highway 99 eastbound at Long Creek Bridge. Flooding was a few feet deep.
Roadway flooding in Vina at Squaw Hill Rd. and South Ave.
Flooding in North Highlands on 3617 Quinn Way due to leaves in the storm drain. The street was flooded.
Highway 36 was flooded at Dales Station.
Roadway flooding in Sacramento on southbound Highway 99 near Sutterville Rd. Water was as deep as car doors and traffic was backed up.
Dry Creek Rd. and Interstate 80 road flooding.
Roadway flooding at Douglas Blvd. and Sierra College Blvd. West bound lanes had two feet of water.
Roadway at Coleman Fish Hatchery Rd. and Gover Rd completely flooded and impassable.
Flooding in southbound Highway 49 just north of 193 in Placerville caused traffic to swerve into northbound lanes.
New Long Valley Road was closed for several hours in the morning following a rock and mud slide.
A slide at Lakeside Heights over topped the K-railing that was placed at the base of the slope and extended out into Hill Road, blocking an access to Sutter Lakeside Hospital.
Flooding was reported in Clearlake, bringing significant and widespread damage. Neighborhoods were evacuated. Roads were damaged. Extensive road repair and debris removal was required.
There were 5 to 11 homes with minor flooding in Nord.
There were 25 homes with minor flooding in Palermo.
Two apartment buildings suffered flooding as a creek behind the buildings over topped.  Residents were forced to evacuate.
Highway 99 was down to one lane due to flooding.
Heavy rain caused closures on Highway 99W between CR 33 and 48, and portions of County Roads 33, 35, 48, Rd D just north of Willows.
County Roads DD, E, FF, and G had closures due to flooding.

There were closures numerous roads near Tehama City, between Red Bluff and Corning. These include Rawson Road-North of Gyle Road, Rawson Road-between Corona Ave and Chittenden, Rawson Road-between Dusty Way and Chard Ave,|Cone Grove Road, Christian Road, Ingraham Road, Woodland Avenue, Tehama Avenue,|Flores Avenue, Capay Road, Shasta Boulevard between 8th and 62nd, Craig Avenue|Hamilton Avenue (Gerber Area), Corning Road (Rawson Road to Black Butte), Bray Avenue, Electric Avenue, Barham Avenue at Finnell Avenue, Gyle Road from Hwy 99w through the City of Tehama, and Kauffman Avenue.
There were 19 inches of wet, heavy snow measured 3 miles ENE of Soda Springs. Heavy snow fell over 18 hours.
There were 13 inches of snow measured at the top of Kirkwood Meadows Mountain Resort, 10 inches at the base at 7200 feet.
There were 10 inches of snowfall total measured at Baxter.
There was a storm total of 9.21 inches of rain that fell through the event, 3.68 inches fell in the last 24 hours.
There were 7 inches of snow measured at 2NW of Almanor, at 5464 feet. Heavy snow fell for 12 hours.
Snow began to stick around 1600 on 12/10/14 in the town of Twain (2800 ft elevation). There were 6 inches of snow measured at 7 am.
Flooding was reported over numerous streets in northern Stockton.
There were 14.8 inches of snow measured at Blue Canyon. Winds gusted up to 69 mph, recorded at 08:00 on December 11, 2015.
Highway 113 at Covell Blvd off ramp had the right lane closed due to a washout.

An 8 ft diameter, 30-40 ft tall grey pine tree fell onto a home in Redding. This home was located on Wyatt Lane, off Churn Creek Road, north of South Bonnyview Road. An adult female was killed, and an male adult and a female toddler(3 yrs of age) were injured in the incident. The Redding Municipal Airport reported NNE winds sustained at 29 mph with gusts to 38 mph at 2 am. The airport is 3.82 mile SSE of the incident. Strong wind duration estimated at about 30 minutes.
Numerous trees and powerlines were knocked down in Paradise and Magalia. There were over 3000 customers without power. Winds gusted to 66 mph at Jarbo Gap at 11:13  PST.
A 2 foot diameter tree was reported down on road 4 miles west of Red Bluff.
Dixon Avenue closed at Pedrick Rd. due to three power lines down over the road. Gusts to 44 mph were measured at Davis University Airport at 9:20 am.

Law enforcement, media, and the public reported numerous trees and large branches downed by winds in Sacramento and adjacent suburbs, such as Rosemont, Carmichael, and Florin. These caused local power outages spread across the area. There was a 38 mph gust measured at 7 am at Sacramento Executive Airport, a 40 mph gust at Sacramento International Airport.
Law enforcement reported a number of trees down on Marysville Rd in Dobbins.
Multiple homes suffered flooding as Deer Creek flooded.  Residents were forced to evacuate.
Winds were 38 mph, gusting to 69 at Blue Canyon at 7:52 AM on 12/12/14.
A strong wind storm brought down trees and power lines, damaging 3 homes in Kyburz.
At least 2 homes badly damaged by falling trees in Grass Valley and Nevada City.
At least 2 homes badly damaged by falling trees in Grass Valley and Nevada City.

Numerous trees reported down in the Sacramento area. Trees were reported falling on homes and business in Sacramento, Elk Grove, and Folsom. Power lines were downed in multiple locations, causing power outages.

Impacts to the region included: Reservoirs dropped to low levels (record lows in some cases), farmers limited plantings of some crops and allowed areas of land to go fallow, increased agricultural unemployment and poverty, strong conservation efforts within many communities, increased reliance on shrinking groundwater resources, a decrease in snow-related tourism activity in the Northern Sierra Nevada, and a large increase in fire danger across the Northern Sierra Nevada, Southern Cascades and Coastal Range. Large wildfires such as the King Fire required large scale and very expensive suppression efforts. |For the entire state of California, 2014 was the warmest on record, which further increased the need for water and reduced an already limited snow pack. The Sierra snow pack ended the year at only about half of normal levels.|The California Department of Food and Agriculture���s Office of Public Relations summarized 2014 California agricultural losses: Direct costs to agriculture total $1.5 billion (revenue losses of $1 billion and $0.5 billion in additional pumping costs). This net revenue loss is about 3 percent of the state���s total agricultural value. The total statewide economic cost of the 2014 drought is $2.2 billion. The loss of 17,100 seasonal and part-time jobs related to agriculture represents 3.8 percent of farm unemployment. About 428,000 acres, or 5 percent, of irrigated cropland went out of production in the Central Valley, Central Coast and Southern California due to the drought.|The UC Davis Center for Watershed Sciences research suggests that northern interior California lost 4115 to 6796 agricultural jobs in 2014. Almond production dropped by 15 percent compared to the 2013. Almonds are the largest crop for the region.

A significant drought continues to impact to the region for January, including a large reduction in snow related tourism in the Northern Sierra Nevada. Multiple downhill and cross country ski resorts were forced to close due to a lack of snow. Resorts which remained open were forced to produce artificial snow, and scale back the number of runs open. Other winter activities such as snowmobiling and snow shoeing were also greatly affected by the lack of snow pack. Restaurants and hotels in the area which rely on winter tourism suffered a significant drop in business.||Many farmers are already planning to scale back crop planting acreage due to decreased irrigation water allocations again in 2015.
Very heavy rain fell over 1.5 hours.
There was 3.31 inches of rain measured over a period of 24 hours.
There was 7.87 inches of rain (storm total) which was measured over a period of 3 days.
CHP reported flooding at the intersection of Highway 99 west and Road 48.
There was 7.77 inches of rain measured over 3 days, with a trace of snow.
There were 1.15 inches of rain measured over 24 hours, with a storm total of 2.70 inches.
Storm total about 5 inches February 5th through 6th.

Impacts to the region for February included strong conservation efforts within most communities, a decrease in the snow-related tourism activity in the Northern Sierra Nevada, reduction in air quality due to persistent stagnant air, and a reduction of ground water resources which are replacing diminished reservoir water. Farmers planned to reduce planting acreage due to projected reduction in irrigation water allocations.
Winds gusted to 82 mph at Soldier Mountain RAWS at 10 AM PST. Widespread tree damage was reported in northeastern Shasta County.
Winds gusted to 76 mph at Cashman RAWS at 10 AM PST. Widespread tree damage was reported in Lassen Volcanic National Park, with potentially thousands of trees downed.

Significant traffic delays occurred on Interstate 80 when a period of heavy snow caused several big rigs to slide and block Donner Pass, with long traffic backups resulting. Many cars were ill prepared for winter driving conditions and multiple car accidents were reported. CHP reported that 1000 cars needed to be turned around due to no chains or studded tires.
There was 9.5 inches of new snow measured at Kingvale, 24 hour total.
Weather spotter measured a wind gust of 52 mph at Fall River Mills. Multiple large trees snapped off or uprooted. A few trees fell into homes. A large pine fell across a mobile home in Macarthur.

Impacts to the region for March included conservation efforts within most foothill communities. Increased water conservation measures were passed by the state to increase reductions further by limiting water use for lawn watering and added incentives to limit water use in hotels and restaurants  There was a continued reduction of ground water resources which are being used to replace diminished reservoir water. Agricultural impacts included orchard reduction, limits on planting and increased costs due to reliance on groundwater. Sutter County alone has lost an estimated 1100 agriculture related jobs. The Lake Don Pedro Community (La Grange and Coulterville)  adopted mandatory water conservation measures and water use restrictions effective March 9th due to the drought emergency and severe lack of water supply in Lake McClure, which is expected to go dry this summer.

The drought is strongly impacting the northern San Joaquin Valley, with farmers reducing acres planted and removing some trees from orchards. Agricultural jobs and businesses related to agriculture have lost jobs. Air quality has suffered, with particulate levels at the highest levels in a decade for some locations.

The drought is impacting the southern Sacramento Valley, with farmers reducing acres planted and removing some trees from orchards. An example of this is rice acreage, which has been cut back by about 25 percent. Agricultural jobs and related businesses have lost jobs. Air quality has suffered, with particulate levels at the highest levels in a decade for some locations.

The drought is impacting the northern Sacramento Valley, with farmers reducing acres planted and removing some trees from orchards. Agricultural jobs and related businesses have lost jobs. Air quality has suffered, with particulate levels at the highest levels in a decade for some locations.
There was a large decrease in the snow-related tourism activity in the Northern Sierra Nevada due to a well below normal snow pack. Many ski resorts ended their seasons early and shut down in March.

The drought is impacting the central Sacramento Valley, with farmers reducing acres planted and removing some trees from orchards. An example of this is rice acreage, which has been cut back by about 25 percent. Agricultural jobs and related businesses have lost jobs. Air quality has suffered, with particulate levels at the highest levels in a decade for some locations.

The drought continues to impact Lake County, with farmers clipping some wine grape vines, reducing irrigation needed this summer, while reducing their harvest. Agriculture and related businesses have lost jobs.

There was a large decrease in the snow-related tourism activity in the Northern Sierra Nevada due to a well below normal snow pack. Many ski resorts ended their seasons early in April, or had already shut down in March.

Locally strong winds caused numerous trees to fall on buildings, vehicles, and power lines in southern Redding. About 20 calls for separate wind damage events were received by emergency responders. At least 4 homes and a garage were struck by falling trees, some seriously damaged. Several cars were also damaged by falling trees and limbs. Power lines were downed in multiple locations, causing power outages for about 600 customers. One power line was reported to have caused a structural fire. Drought stressed trees were reported to be a significant factor in the damage by power company crews.

Caltrans measured a total of 8 inches of snow at Kingvale at 6100 ft. Up to 14 inches of snow was measured at Echo Summit. This snow brought chain restrictions, accidents, and slow traffic on I80 and Highway 50. Small hail from thunderstorms caused travel accidents along Highway 49.
Quarter size hail was reported in the town of North San Juan.
There were 1.75 inches of rain that fell overnight at Drum Forebay.
Heavy rain reported, 1.66 inches storm total.
Spotter reported 1.62 inches of rain over the last 24 hours.There were 0.30 inches of rain within the last hour, with some snow mixed in.
Heavy rain reported, 1.57 inches storm total.
Heavy rain reported., 1.10 inches storm total.
Heavy rain reported., 1.18 storm total.
Heavy rain reported by NWS employee, 1.19 inches storm total.
A weather spotter measured a storm total of 9 inches of snow, 1.12 inches of snow water equivalent.
A weather spotter measured a storm total of 13 inches of new snow.
A possible funnel cloud was sited at Marconi Ave. and the Capital City Expressway.
A driver along Interstate 5 saw a funnel cloud with a thunderstorm. It is unclear if it touched the ground.
The 24 hour rain total through 4 pm was0.67 inches.
The 24 hour total rain was 0.92 inches, 0.21 inches since 9 am.
The 24 hour total rain was 0.86 inches.
The 24 hour total rain was 1.07 inches.

Snow caused slippery roads on mountains and passes above 6500 feet, with 7 inches of snow measured 3W of Shriner Lake Campground. Golf ball hail was reported southeast of Quincy, in the vicinity of the Minerva Fire.

A 13-year-old was hospitalized Tuesday after suffering heat stroke during tryouts for the freshman football team at Lincoln High School on August 1. Temperatures at Lincoln Airport reached 100 degrees between 4 and 7 pm PDT.
Hail covered the ground. Some of the hail stones were as large as an inch in diameter.
Nickel size hail, strong gusty wind and lightning strikes reported. Event time estimated by radar.
Hail stones accumulated on Highway 88, as large as an inch in diameter.

A large tree in near Sutter's Fort fell across L and 26th streets in Sacramento. Two people sitting at a nearby bus stop were hit by branches. They were transported to the hospital and treated for minor injuries. Wind gusts reached as high as 49 mph at Sacramento International Airport.

There were 398 structures destroyed, 203 residences, 194 outbuildings & 1 commercial structure. Clear Lake supplies municipal water for several communities.|Wind gusts were up to 63 mph 8 miles ENE Hidden Valley Lake,  50 mph 1 mile SSE Wilbur Springs,   45 mph 5 miles E Talmage.

There was 8.21 of rain reported at 2 NE American House over 72 hours.

events.event_narrative: Snow brought travel problems to Highway 299, with chain controls at Buckhorn Summit.

Snow brought travel problems and several hours of chain controls to Interstate 5 over far northern Shasta County. An inch of snow was reported down to Lakehead at 1500 feet elevation, with light accumulations down to 1200 feet at O'Brien.  There was 6.5 of snow reported 5 miles northwest of Mt. Shasta.
A storm total of about 30 of snow was measured at Lower Lassen Peak at 8250 feet. Chain controls were put in effect on Highways 70 and 89.
Snow brought travel slowdowns and chain controls to I80 and Highway 50, with 7 of new snow measured at Kingvale, 9 at Donner Pass, 10 at Soda Springs.
Winds brought down trees and branches causing power outages. Nearly 13,000 customers were without power in the Sacramento area, about 5,000 in Davis.
There was 1.30 rain measured in Oroville over 24 hours.
Rain fell over the area.

A rotating wall cloud with a funnel cloud was reported by a trained spotter, viewed just to the southwest of Loma Rica. No contact with the ground was observed. Pea size hail was also reported with this storm.
A trained spotter reported a total of 24 of snow at Kingvale, between January 24-26.

Caltrans reported a total of 20 of snow at Soda Springs, between January 24-26. This brought chain controls to mountain freeways such as I80 and Highway 50, with vehicle spin outs, and long travel delays.||Ski resorts reported heavy snow, with storm totals of 24 at Squaw Valley, 23 at Tahoe Donner, 20 at Boreal, 18 at Sugar Bowl, and 12 at Bear Valley.

Low elevation snow impacted Highway 299 and 70 with chain controls and delays.  Snotel at Lower Lassen Peak at 8250' reported 19 of snow. Coop observer at Chester reported 7 of snow, with 4 falling in just 2 hours.  There was 1 of snow measured at Shingletown.

Snow brought travel slowdowns and chain controls to Highway 299, with 7 of new snow measured at Lower Lassen Peak, 1 at Shingletown.

Temperatures at Crabtree Weather Station reached 24 on the 19th, 22 on the 20th, 25 on the 21st. Temperatures at Stockton Metropolitan Airport reached 28 on the 20th and 21st.

Snow caused chain controls and travel delays in the Sierra, with road sensor data showing speeds briefly dropping to around 15 mph on I80 near pass level on the 19th and again on the 22nd. Caltrans reported 6 of snow at Soda Springs, 3 at Kingvale. Kirkwood Ski Resort reported 10 of new snow. Other reports include 6 at Bear Valley Ski Resort, 6 at Squaw-Alpine Ski Resort, 5 at Sugar Bowl Ski Resort, 4 at Tahoe Donner Ski Resort, and 2 at Dodge Ridge Ski Resort.
Snow caused travel delays in the northeast foothills. A weather spotter reported a trace of new snow in Paradise. Lower Lassen Peak reported 4 of new snow.

Low elevation snow caused minor travel delays in the Motherlode. Weather spotters reported 1 of snow in Placerville, a trace at Shingle Springs(elevations 1400 feet), and a trace in Auburn (elevation 1500 feet).

Large amounts of small hail blanketed downtown and northern Sacramento, Natomas, and adjacent portions of I5, causing major traffic problems during the afternoon commute. Hail fell 2 to 4 inches deep in portions of north Sacramento and Natomas. Snow plows were required to remove hail in some areas. |Some damage was done to awnings and parking lot covers. The California State Library roof suffered damage and leaked, with hundreds of rare books soaked with water.
At least one funnel cloud was reported near Sacramento International Airport. No touchdown or damage was observed.

A spotter at Quincy observed 11.5 of new snow, elevation 3600 feet. Chain controls and travel delays were reported in the area.

A spotter reported 14 of snow at Kingvale, with .85 liquid equivalent. Caltrans reported 20 of snow at Castle Peak. Chain controls and significant delays were experienced on mountain highways such as I80 and Highway 50. Kyburz had 4 of new snow.
A weather spotter at Sims reported 3 of snow, elevation 2500 feet. A trace of snow was also reported at Lakehead, elevation 1600 feet. This caused minor delays on I5 and mountain roads.
Heavy rain fell. The 24 hour total rainfall was 1.63.
The 24 hour total rainfall was 1.60. Some wet snow mixed in at times.

Major travel disruptions occurred from very heavy snow coupled with gusty winds. Whiteout conditions prompted the closure of a 70-mile stretch of I80 in both directions, from around noon to 3 pm on March 1. Highway 88 near the Kirkwood ski resort was also shut down for several hours. Caltrans road sensors also recorded significant delays and major slow downs on I80 on March 4th. Highway 50 and other mountain highways were also heavily impacted with chain controls and slowdowns. ||Caltrans reported the following 24 hour snow totals at Donner Summit (elevation 7,239 feet) on I80: 8 on March 1, 18 on March 2, 8 on March 3, 8 on March 4, for a storm total of 62. There was a storm total of 58 measured at Kingvale, elevation 6100 feet.||Accumulating snow was reported down into the lower Sierra, with a storm total of 13 at Camino (3100 feet).
Travel disruptions occurred from periods of heavy snow, with chain controls and slowdowns. Plumas County schools were closed. Lower Lassen Peak reported 28 of new snow on March 2, Quincy 5.
Dime sized hail was reported in Corning, CA.
Public reported accumulating hail up to 2 inches deep on roads in central Tehama County.
There was 1.91 inches of rain measured over 12 hours.
Public reported accumulating hail up to 2 inches deep on roads in central Tehama County, including Highway 99.

Heavy snow fell, impacting travel on Sierra Highways with chain controls, holds, and closures for elevations above 3000'. There was 35 of new snow at Sierra at Tahoe, 32 of new snow at Kirkwood Ski Resort, 41 at Squaw Alpine Ski Resort, 42 at the Caltrans Kingvale Maintenance Yard, 16 at Echo Peak, 14 at Blue Canyon. Numerous road closures were reported, including I80 east of Applegate due to heavy snow, Carson Pass/SR-88 and Hwy 50 between Twin Bridges and Meyers for avalanche control, Hwy 89 between Truckee an d Alpine Meadows due to a collision involving 20 vehicles, Hwy 50 eastbound at Sly Park Rd, westbound of Meyers due to snow downed power lines, and Hwy 20 east of Nevada City due to heavy snow.
Heavy snow fell, impacting travel on mountain roads with chain controls and delays. There was 7 of new snow at Quincy.
Combie road flooded due to overtopping of the adjacent Ragsdale Creek.
Closed lanes on Highway 50 at Latrobe Rd/El Dorado Hills due to rockslide.
Street flooding on Dean Way east of Wales Dr. in Folsom.
Street flooding in Cameron Park Estates Mobile Home Park. Video via Twitter.
Vehicle stuck in a flooded roadway on Scott Rd. and Latrobe Rd.

Extensive flooding in downtown Groveland, as floodwaters ran down the main street, Highway 120. Property was damage and water rescues for stranded residents. There was significant damage done to Groveland Community Hall and Mary Laveroni Community Park. Preliminary estimates from Tuolumne County are approximately $8 million for 16 damaged sites along county maintained roads. A very large portion of these damages are seen in the sinkhole at Ferretti Road and slides and embankment loss on Priest Coulterville Road.
A funnel cloud was observed, weakening. Dime size hail was also observed.
A funnel cloud was observed, extending halfway to the ground.

Tornado touchdown observed by Yuba County deputies at Yuba County. Minor damage was observed, including ripped tarps and objects knocked over. Another touchdown was observed and videoed in an open field, about a mile to the north. No damage was observed at the second touchdown location.

A period of heavy rain upstream from Moccasin Dam, in which about three inches fell during four hours led to significant erosion and at least one landslide. It caused a massive amount of water and debris to run downhill into the Moccasin Reservoir. The water level rose to 3 times the normal reservoir capacity and the emergency spillway was utilized. There was severe erosion of the emergency spillway and potential for the dam to fail.  The Power house and staff at the Moccasin Fish Hatchery were evacuated due to potential failure. All the fish in the Moccasin Creek Hatchery were killed when it flooded from the water coming over the emergency spillway.  The National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning associated with the probable dam failure, and the sheriff advised residents to avoid the area as a matter of public safety. The warning was reduced to a watch until the reservoir was drained and then the watch was canceled once the reservoir was drained.||Cleanup and repair efforts associated with a major storm that damaged Tuolumne County's Moccasin Creek Dam in March is expected to cost roughly $43 million, according to an estimate by the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, which owns and operates the dam. That total includes $3.2 million in damage to the state fish hatchery at Moccasin Creek, which lies downstream.

Heavy snow fell, causing travel slowdowns disruptions over higher elevations of mountain highways including I80 and Highway 50. At Kirkwood Ski Resort, a storm total of 32 of new snow was reported, 31 at North Star, 24 at Sierra at Tahoe. There was 8 of new snow at Kingvale, elevation 6100'.
There were 5 vehicles involved in an accident attributed to dense fog. There were 7 injuries reported.

A mother and son died after returning from a day of skiing to their vacation condominium in Kirkwood. A chunk of snow about the size of a trailer fell from the roof of their vacation condominium, burying them under about 3 feet of snow.

Heavy rain caused a railroad bridge in Marysville to sink. The bridge spans the Yuba River. Rail traffic over the bridge was shut down. A diesel pipeline attached to the bridge also had to be shut down. Union Pacific Railroad drove in new piles to stabilize the bridge. Repairs were completed on March 27.

Roadway flooding was reported at Lower Honcut Road and Ramirez Road.
